_<font face="Times New Roman">It began in New Mexico. And while it's been said that any journey that begins in Albuquerque is doomed to failure, this adventure began further north than that... in TAOS!</font>_

  

## Into the Southwest, Pt I

by **San Jaya Prime**

How do I even put this into words? It happened the very first time I hit Taos coming out of Colorado -- _that's_ when the Southwest finally hit me. _That's_ when I caught my first real glimmer of what this land actually is.

These tracks weren't birthed in some sterile studio. They were built piece by piece from pure, scattered moments. Sitting in the back of a banged-up trailer hunched over a keyboard next to Tunzer, trying to stitch together raw soundscapes. Sitting on a hard rock floor with Megan, drumming out broken beats and humming in the dirt. Lying out with Nikki, the fallen angel, on a busted fold-out bed, singing music that had never even been written down. Sitting over a groovebox with Zero and Egg for endless hours over bad coffee at an IHOP and never wanting the night to end. Or just posting up on the slopes near Fort Mason with Jade and breadbowls still warm, staring out at the sands in the distance and humming along with the ocean as our beat and our rhythm. All of it bled directly into the music.

texts: "The sky wasn't just blue... it was the color of a forgotten god's faded jeans, threading at the knees from too much kneeling to mend their mistakes."
\- Kantiki Jayamana, on New Mexico, Landlore

content.text:
### The Road Venues + The Band

At first, they were just melodies in my head, with different souls adding their own pieces along the way. We sang some of these at the long-lost Sedona hostel. We belted others from the stairs in San Diego for Annie's birthday at a hostel that'll never open its doors again.

We even dragged a few of these onto the stage over the years, and man... my poor band members. They'd show up expecting proper sheet music, and instead, they got me saying, "Well, it goes a little like this," before I'd just start beatboxing, humming, and verbally inserting harmonies.

Then Nikki introduced me to Jade out in San Francisco's Chinatown. This was back when the old Fort Mason hostel still stared down Alcatraz, back when you could walk out back and smoke a cigarette with your morning coffee. The first time I heard her play the cello was incredible, but realizing she could wield a mandolin like a classical Spanish guitar? That was a straight-up gift to the world. That... _that_ is fucking magic!

We'd play these tracks live whenever we could somehow wrangle everyone together, but they never quite fit into any of my official series. Not into IO, not into my "Study in Forces" DJ mixes. They were... well, yeah, effectively homeless. Kinda fitting really.

### The Landscape's Grip

But the Southwest stayed with me. It sank its teeth in. I pushed into the Nevada deserts and became a connoisseur of sand and arid air. I crossed into Utah, where the landscape literally grabbed my heart, stole my breath, and dragged me onto a completely different plane of existence. Or out under the Arizona sky, driving with LiLi Glitch, never expecting the horizon to suddenly erupt with a massive crest of satellites aimed at the heavens -- with the satellites just quietly listening, holding onto that silent, desperate hope for a signal telling us we aren't alone.

From the treacherous drive down across Colorado into Texas, watching the dirty sands give way to the marshy East... the Southwest is always with me. It marked me. It changed my life forever. From riding in the back of Mario's truck with his sons across the Jicarilla reservation while bison turned the ground beneath our tires into an earthquake, to the impossibly shimmering White Sands, to the thriving, chaotic market festivals of Santa Fe. Over and over again. Scar by scar. Note by note. Piece by little piece.

texts: "Any journey that starts with the thought that you shouldn't've moved the peyote is bound to end in neon jellyfish swimming through desert skies. It's effectively predestined, right?"

content.text:
### Hippie Folklore

What some folks don't realize is that when you're trekking deep into the mountains or out in the heavy forests where no one else is around, you sing. You sing loudly, putting your full lungs behind every damned note. It's infinitely better to let the wildlife know you're coming than to walk up and surprise an animal you really don't wanna surprise.

So, I've sung every one of these songs over and over, in a hundred different ways. The cuts on this album? They're just one way to hear them. These are tracks born straight from the dirt of the road, from the festival grounds, and from the drum circles where Ra, Nugget, and myself first played them live out at the Tucson Gem Show.

At this point, they've mutated into pure hippie folklore. I'm probably not even the only one singing them anymore. Are they my creations? Indeed they are. But in so many ways, they were gifted to me, instilled in me, and inspired by everything around me.

_They belong to you just as much as they belong to me._

That said, Arizona wine is better than Napa. End of story.

### The Art + The Illusions

Some of the hardcore fans actually saw a completely different, early version of the cover art back when I was dropping the originals state-by-state on Bandcamp. I took the surreal maps from each of those covers and stitched them together into one massive whole. But it had this weird, chaotic effect. There was so much visual noise that it just turned into static... honestly, it was almost boring.

So, I ripped it apart. I twisted the perspective, laid down some hard outlines, and started building the new art straight over the wreckage. I pulled in the same stippling technique I sometimes use in my photography -- pushing it closer to a halftone vibe -- and definitely leaned heavy on M C Escher for some of those illusions.

Looking back, I love how it turned out -- except for two glaring details that still eat at me. First, I never should've compromised on the flag. I already have two of my own custom Jolly Rogers ("Punk Is Dead" from [_Warriors in Waiting_](#?/warriors-in-waiting-live-set) and "Tao of the Criminal"). But at the time, I watered it down because I wanted it to be easily identifiable. Huge mistake. Second, the pathway lines. I should've textured them -- just some halftone and stippling -- and cranked them to a slightly steeper tilt. Nobody else has ever pointed these out, so I'm pretty sure it's just a me-thing, but it still grinds my gears.

### Living Storybook Songs These songs did not start with the official release in late 2024, nor have they ended there. Hell, some of these go back farther than some of my _IO_ releases. They're living songs, storybooks with history that grows and evolves. In fact, that 2024 release is already two versions behind from some of those that are on Bandcamp. Then even some of the 2025 versions on Bandcamp have already been replaced by 2026 cuts. Any song you hear here is but a polaroid frozen in time. To name just one example, "The Moon on Pandora's Skin" really should be an industrial goth song befitting of that particular creature. I'll one day finally get to that point with the song, whereas for the moment it stands as a two-step mix awaiting that remix. Let's talk production. For that 2024 release, AI did a LOT of the heavy lifting on more than 60% of the music -- specifically Suno AI, Meta's Segment Anything Audio, and ElevenLabs. Feeding them live recordings or humming and beat-boxing them out, then taking what the AI returned and hacking, slashing, and slicing it all to hell to get the samples I needed. The rest was violently hammered out on hardware synthesizers and MPCs, with even more layers salvaged from raw field recordings that I scrubbed clean using SAA. I was handing the machines raw, dirty recordings, and they were giving samples I could pull into the MPC. To my ear, I can distinctly hear the seams between all three of those methods. "Calling Down the Sky" stands out as the prime example; it's an absolute Frankenstein of a track. I've sliced, reorganized, and rebuilt these beats so many times that, at one point, I genuinely lost the plot altogether. Fitting for half the shit I got up to in New Mexico.

texts: "From the bed of a truck, I've seen the unending horizon of the New Mexican Wastelands, the Grasslands of East Texas, and I've picked wheat while driving thru the farms of the Midwest."

content.text:
### The Long + Dusty Road

The final album acts as a rough "best of" compilation from those original EP drops. It pulls four tracks from each leg of the journey: kicking up dust in New Mexico, dragging across Arizona, bleeding into California, pushing up to Nevada, cutting into Utah, dropping down through Colorado, grinding into Texas, and finally closing out with a heavy memoir section.

I thought about doing a tedious, song-by-song breakdown for this release. But honestly? Nah. I'll leave that up to the folks who've read _"[Landlore](landlore)"_ to make their own guesses on exactly where each track belongs. Besides, I think the songs tell their own stories well enough.

### Extended Listening + Exploration ### \[[Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/album/5KbEUOcYx9MSFuY1VBeM9B?si=Kdqy2hKeSBOZo_OXUQdScw)\] \[[Apple Music](https://music.apple.com/ca/album/into-the-southwest-pt-i/1778781741)\] \[[YouTube Music](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p4-oyzNHcCU&list=OLAK5uy_nf4oz0UgmyWyEtSSohkxwLqXugJbXNG6U&index=1)\] The main release, "Into the Southwest, Pt I" is that polaroid photo frozen in time that acts of a "best of" collection for the various state-by-state EPs I released from the series. Not all of the original cuts made it to the album. To keep up with the living series as it evolves, you'll want to tune into the series here on Bandcamp: 1. _In2SW: New Mexico, Pt I_ ([Bandcamp](https://sanjayaprime.bandcamp.com/album/new-mexico-part-i)) 2. _In2SW: Arizona, Pt I_ ([Bandcamp](https://sanjayaprime.bandcamp.com/album/arizona-part-i)) 3. _In2SW: California, Pt I_ ([Bandcamp](https://sanjayaprime.bandcamp.com/album/california-part-i)) 4. _In2SW: Nevada, Pt I_ ([Bandcamp](https://sanjayaprime.bandcamp.com/album/nevada-part-i)) 5. _In2SW: Utah, Pt I_ ([Bandcamp](https://sanjayaprime.bandcamp.com/album/utah-part-i)) 6. _In2SW: Colorado, Pt I_ ([Bandcamp](https://sanjayaprime.bandcamp.com/album/colorado-part-i)) 7. _In2SW: Texas, Pt I_ ([Bandcamp](https://sanjayaprime.bandcamp.com/album/texas-part-i)) And of course, if you want to hear a few live versions of these, then I was able to clean up some of the originals and get them on the "[Warriors in Waiting](warriors-in-waiting-live-set)" set. And yes, that includes the standing ovation live cut of "El Camino Real" where Jade took center stage. In all honesty, I shouldn't've kept Doc in that set, as it was beyond repair, but it has personal significance to the point where I wasn't going to cut it out.
